beats.intro: Lesson twenty-eight. [[sub]]Two emotionally charged tasks close this part of the book. First: interviewing someone you might hire.
beats.why: An interview has four purposes. [[sel]]Select a good performer. [[edu]]Teach the candidate who you are. [[match]]Check that the match works both ways. [[sell]]And sell them on the job. [[means]]Your tools: an hour or two of talk, and a reference check. [[hard]]Appraising your own reports is hard, after months beside them. Here you get an hour to predict how a stranger will do somewhere new. [[imp]]If appraisal is difficult, interviewing is just about impossible. [[risk]]Do it anyway, knowing the risk is high.
beats.talk: Who talks? [[eighty]]The candidate, about eighty percent of the time. [[ctrl]]But you steer, as an active listener. [[on]]A nervous or chatty person may run on, and out of courtesy we sit and listen. [[cut]]Don't. The hour is your only asset. Interrupt, apologize if you like, and change the subject. [[yours]]The interview is yours to control. If you don't, you have only yourself to blame.
beats.common: You learn most on ground you both know. [[self]]Let them talk about what they did, why, and what they would do differently. [[terms]]But in terms familiar to you, so you can judge it. [[words]]Make sure the words mean the same thing to both of you.
beats.questions: What to ask? [[group]]A group of managers gave Grove their best questions. [[q1]]Which projects did your management value, even above your boss? [[q2]]Your weaknesses, and how you work on them? [[q3]]Why should we hire you? [[q4]]Your current problems: how are you solving them, and how could you have prevented them? [[q5]]Why are you ready for this job? [[q6]]Your biggest achievements, and why? [[q7]]Your biggest failures, and what you learned? [[q8]]Why should an engineer move into marketing? Adjust that one to the job. [[q9]]And your most important college project?
beats.four: The answers give four kinds of information. [[tech]]Technical skill: not science, but skill at this job. Accounting for an accountant, tax law for a tax lawyer, statistics for an actuary. [[did]]What they did with what they know. [[gap]]The reasons for any gap between knowing and doing. [[val]]And their operational values, which would guide them on the job. [[sort]]Grove sorts the nine questions into those four groups.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which kind of information does each question get at?
beats.potential: In the end you are judging how this person would perform in your company. [[trap]]In performance reviews, Grove warns against rating potential. [[must]]In hiring, potential is exactly what you must judge. [[bridge]]You project their future in your world from their own account of their past. [[self]]So you rely on self-assessment, and that is fine. [[ask]]Ask straight out: how good are you technically? A pause, then a modest, pretty good. You get a decent fix. [[direct]]Don't worry about being blunt. Direct questions bring direct answers, or other insight.
beats.hypo: A hypothetical can show a lot. [[cand]]Grove once interviewed a Harvard business graduate from the food industry, for cost accountant at Intel. [[none]]He knew nothing about chips; Grove knew nothing about finance. [[walk]]So Grove walked him through chip making, offered to answer any question, [[wafer]]and asked: what does a finished wafer cost? [[think]]The candidate thought it through, working out cost accounting principles as he went. [[right]]He got the right answer and was hired. His problem-solving proved first-rate.
beats.theirq: Another approach: [[turn]]ask what the candidate wants to know about you, the company, or the job. [[shows]]Their questions show what they know, what they want to know, and how well they prepared. [[fool]]Not foolproof, though. One prospective manager brought Grove an annual report marked up with sharp questions, many Grove couldn't answer. [[fail]]Impressed, they hired him. He failed badly.
beats.refs: Now references. [[same]]You want the same information you sought from the candidate. [[strange]]A stranger's praise means little if you don't know their company's values. And few references lie, but few volunteer criticism. [[know]]A reference you know gives real information. [[bond]]With a stranger, stay on the phone until some bond forms. Find a shared experience. [[last]]Grove found the last ten minutes of a half-hour call worth far more than the first ten. [[again]]Then, if you can, meet the candidate again, briefly and with focus.
beats.tricks: What about tricks? [[rick]]Admiral Rickover, the story goes, sat navy submarine candidates on a chair with a short leg. When it tipped, they sprawled on the floor: a test of character, he thought. [[straight]]Grove's view: be completely straightforward. [[first]]Candidates leave with strong first impressions, and if you hire them, those last a long time. [[real]]So show yourself and your workplace as they really are.
beats.luck: Are there guarantees? [[hire]]Grove once interviewed for a senior post as carefully as he could, and felt he understood the person well. [[day]]From day one, the hire was a disaster. [[notes]]Humbled, he reread his notes and the reference calls. He still has no idea what he missed. [[odds]]Careful interviewing guarantees nothing. It only improves your odds of getting lucky.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]An interview selects, teaches, checks the match, and sells. [[w2]]They talk eighty percent; you control the hour. [[w3]]Probe skill, what they did, gaps, and values. [[w4]]Ask directly, try a hypothetical, work the references. [[w5]]Be straightforward. Care only improves your odds. Now the lesson practice.
beats.final1: Lesson practice. Five situations from a manager's week.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty-eight. Next, the other difficult task: a valued person who says, I quit.
